sources.extracted_text: New model scheduling · Ollama Blog New model scheduling September 23, 2025 Ollama now includes a significantly improved model scheduling system. Ahead of running a model, Ollama’s new engine will now measure the exact amount of memory required compared to an estimation in previous versions of Ollama. This has several benefits: Significantly reduced crashes due to out of memory issues: Because memory management is exact, over-allocations no longer occur meaning fewer out of memory issues. Maximizing GPU utilization: Ollama’s new memory management allocates more memory to the GPU, increasing token generation and processing speeds Multi-GPU performance: Ollama will now schedule models more efficiently over multiple GPUs, significantly improving multi-GPU and mismatched GPU performance Accurate reporting: Measurements in tools like nvidia-smi will now match ollama ps making it easy to track memory utilization on your system All models implemented in Ollama’s new engine now have this new feature enabled by default, with more models coming soon as they transition to Ollama’s new engine. A No‑Hype Review Is Ollama the Best Local LLM Runner in 2025? A No‑Hype Review Updated at Sep 17, 2025 8 min Is Ollama the Best Local LLM Runner in 2025? A No‑Hype Review If you’ve ever wished ChatGPT‑style power without the cloud, Ollama might be your new favorite tool. It turns your laptop or workstation into a fast, private hub for large language models (LLMs)—no account, no usage caps, and your data never leaves your machine. But is Ollama really the best way to run local LLMs in 2025? This review breaks down what it does well, where it falls short, and how it stacks up in the growing local‑AI ecosystem. In this Ollama review, we’ll cover features, performance, model support, developer experience, privacy, and alternatives—plus hands‑on guidance to help you decide if it’s right for you. ﻿ ﻿ : Ollama Review Verdict Best for : Developers, tinkerers, and privacy‑first teams who want local LLMs with minimal setup. What it nails : Simple CLI/daemon, one‑line model pulls, broad model support, offline use, fast on Apple Silicon, growing Windows/Linux support. Where it lags : GUI is minimal (third‑party UIs help), VRAM limits big models, multi‑GPU and fine‑tuning options are basic, model management can be manual. Alternatives : LM Studio (polished desktop UI), vLLM (server inference at scale), text‑generation‑webui (flexible but complex), KoboldCPP (lightweight), Oobabooga (power user features). Strong head‑to‑head with LM Studio in 2025 coverage. ﻿ What Is Ollama, Exactly? Ollama is a local LLM runtime and model manager. You install it, run a background service, and interact via CLI or an OpenAI‑compatible HTTP endpoint. It downloads and serves quantized models—like Llama‑3, Mistral, Phi‑3, and Gemma—optimized for CPU/GPU so you can chat, embed, or generate code entirely offline. Install and run: ollama run llama3 Pull models: ollama pull mistral Serve an API: ollama serve (then call it like OpenAI) In short, think: “Homebrew for LLMs” with a dead‑simple dev experience. ﻿ Who Is Ollama For? Builders who want to prototype apps locally with an OpenAI‑style API. Security‑conscious teams keeping sensitive prompts/data on‑prem. Researchers comparing models without cloud costs or limits. Power users automating workflows (CLI + local scripts). If you want a one‑click GUI and model browsing, LM Studio may feel friendlier—see 2025 comparisons showing how each fits different user types. ﻿ Key Features: Where Ollama Shines 1) Frictionless Setup and Use One‑line model pulls and runs. Background service exposes a simple REST API. Works across macOS (great on M‑series), Windows, and Linux. 2) Broad Model Library Popular families: Llama‑3/3.1, Mistral/Mixtral, Phi‑3, Gemma, Qwen, Code‑specialized models, and small footprint chat models. Quantized variants (e.g., Q4, Q5, Q8) for different VRAM/CPU budgets. Community‑shared model files via Modelfile recipes. Recent write‑ups highlight Ollama’s role as a privacy‑first runner for modern open models in 2025, with practical developer examples. 3) Offline, Private by Default No external calls unless you add them. Fits GDPR‑sensitive workflows and regulated industries when properly configured. 4) OpenAI‑Compatible Patterns Swap endpoints in your app from OpenAI to local Ollama. Great for cost‑control and prototyping with zero cloud spend. 5) Fast on Apple Silicon, Solid on GPUs M‑series chips run small/medium models smoothly. On NVIDIA GPUs, quantized 7B–13B models can feel real‑time. ﻿ Where Ollama Falls Short Limited native GUI: You’ll often pair it with a web UI or IDE extension. LM Studio wins on UI polish and model discovery UX. VRAM hungry models: 70B models need serious GPU memory or aggressive quantization (quality trade‑offs). Fine‑tuning: Mostly geared to inference; advanced training/fine‑tune workflows require other tools. Multi‑GPU scaling: Improving, but still behind specialized inference servers like vLLM for high‑throughput production. ﻿ Real‑World Performance: What to Expect Performance depends on model size, quantization, and hardware. 3B–7B models: Near‑instant responses for chat, drafting, and light code. 8B–13B: Good balance of quality vs. speed; viable for most local tasks. 30B–70B: Possible but heavy; expect slower tokens, high VRAM needs, or CPU fallback. Articles evaluating 2025 local runners consistently place Ollama among the easiest ways to get great speed/latency on consumer machines, especially for 7B–13B models. For large‑scale serving and throughput, tools like vLLM are often recommended. ﻿ Developer Experience: Smooth and Familiar API Usage POST /api/generate for text generation. POST /v1/chat/completions for OpenAI‑style chat. Streams with server‑sent events; easy to wire into web apps. Modelfile and Prompt Templates Define a base model, system prompt, and adapters. Shareable recipes make experiments reproducible. Simple Local Ops Caching keeps hot models responsive. Versioned pulls let you pin specific builds. Logs are straightforward for debugging. ﻿ Privacy & Security: Why Teams Choose Ollama Data stays local unless you call out to other services. Works well for internal PII, source code, and regulated content with proper governance. Combine with local vector DBs (e.g., SQLite, Chroma) to build private RAG flows. Guides in 2025 emphasize Ollama for GDPR‑aligned data control when used entirely on‑prem. ﻿ Ollama vs. LM Studio (And Others) Here’s the landscape based on recent 2025 comparisons and roundups: LM Studio: Best desktop UI, built‑in chat, easy model browsing. Great for non‑devs. Ollama is leaner, more scriptable, and better as a local service. vLLM: Superior for high‑throughput, multi‑client inference with advanced scheduling. Use for production servers; pair with Ollama for local prototyping. Text‑generation‑webui / Oobabooga: Very flexible, lots of knobs; steeper learning curve. KoboldCPP: Lightweight, story‑writing niche; fast on CPU. Takeaway: Ollama is the best “developer‑first local runtime.” If you need a polished chat app out of the box, LM Studio could fit better. ﻿ Use Cases: What You Can Build Today Secure internal coding assistant using a 7B–13B code model. Private RAG chatbot over company docs with embeddings + local vector DB. On‑device content drafting, translation, and summarization. Rapid prototyping of AI features before committing to cloud costs. Example flow: Pull a model: ollama pull llama3 Embed docs locally, build a vector index. Create a chat endpoint that grounds responses using retrieval. Swap to a larger model if needed, or quantize further for speed. ﻿ Setup Guide: From Zero to First Response Install Ollama for your OS and start the service. Pull a model: ollama pull mistral or ollama run phi3 . Test in terminal: ollama run mistral then chat. Serve API: ollama serve and call ` Integrate in code (Python/JavaScript) using OpenAI‑compatible clients by pointing to your local endpoint. Performance tips: Prefer 4‑bit or 5‑bit quantization for laptops. On Apple Silicon, enable Metal acceleration by default (installed binaries handle this). For NVIDIA GPUs, keep VRAM headroom; disable other VRAM‑heavy apps. ﻿ Pricing: What Does Ollama Cost? The software is free and open‑source to run locally. Your costs are hardware, electricity, and time. For heavier models, invest in more VRAM or an M‑series Mac. Roundups of local‑AI stacks in 2025 often highlight Ollama for being both budget‑friendly and high‑performance for its class. ﻿ Limitations and Gotchas Context windows vary by model; long documents may require chunking and retrieval. Quantization reduces memory but can soften reasoning fidelity; test prompts. Some models require specific licenses or attribution—check before commercial use. Windows GPU paths can need extra drivers/config; macOS is the smoothest. ﻿ Who Should Skip Ollama? Teams needing enterprise‑grade autoscaling, multi‑tenant throughput, and GPU pooling should look at vLLM or managed inference. Content creators who want a polished, integrated chat interface might prefer LM Studio. ﻿ Quick Hands‑On: Calling Ollama Like OpenAI # Start the server ollama serve ﻿ # Simple curl request (chat-style) curl \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "mistral", "messages": [ {"role": "user", "content": "Explain zero-shot learning simply."} ], "stream": true }' ﻿ Should You Use Ollama in 2025? Choose Ollama if you value privacy, speed on consumer hardware, and a clean developer workflow. Pair it with a lightweight UI or your own front end for a great local assistant. If you scale to many users or need a GUI‑first experience, evaluate vLLM or LM Studio in parallel. ﻿ By the way: Supercharge Local AI Workflows with Sider.AI Relevance score: 8/10. If you’re building AI‑assisted research, writing, or coding workflows, it’s worth noting that Sider.AI can slot into your stack as a front‑end companion—drafting content, organizing prompts, and managing context. When paired with a local Ollama backend, you get privacy‑first generation plus a productivity‑focused interface that keeps you in flow. ﻿ Key Takeaways Ollama is the most developer‑friendly local LLM runner for 2025. It’s free, private, and fast for 7B–13B models—ideal for prototyping and secure workflows. LM Studio is better if you want a GUI; vLLM if you need production‑grade serving. Check model licenses, quantize smartly, and test prompts for quality. Start with ollama run llama3 and build from there. FAQ Q1:Is Ollama free to use in 2025? Yes, Ollama is free and open-source to run locally. Your main costs are hardware and time to download and manage models, which is why it’s popular for budget-friendly local LLM setups. Q2:Which models work best with Ollama on a laptop? Quantized 7B–13B models like Llama 3, Mistral, and Phi-3 usually deliver the best balance of speed and quality on laptops, especially on Apple Silicon or NVIDIA GPUs. Q3:How does Ollama compare to LM Studio? Ollama is developer-first with a simple CLI and API, great for scripting and local services. LM Studio offers a polished GUI and easy model discovery, which many non-developers prefer. Q4:Can I replace OpenAI’s API with Ollama locally? Often yes. Ollama exposes an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so you can point your existing client to localhost for private, offline development—then switch back to cloud when needed. Q5:Is Ollama good for enterprise use? It’s excellent for on-prem prototyping and privacy-first workflows. For multi-user, high-throughput serving at scale, pair Ollama with or consider vLLM or managed inference platforms. sources.extracted_text: Why You Should Stop Using Ollama in 2026 and What to Use Instead Agree & Join LinkedIn By clicking Continue to join or sign in, you agree to LinkedIn’s User Agreement , Privacy Policy , and Cookie Policy . Skip to main content Let me start with a confession. I used Ollama for a long time, and I recommended it to almost everyone who asked me about running AI models locally. It deserved that recommendation when it launched. You typed one command, a model loaded, and you had a running LLM on your own hardware with zero configuration. It was genuinely the easiest on-ramp to local inference that existed. That recommendation no longer holds, and I want to explain exactly why, with real numbers rather than vague complaints, because the situation has changed enough in 2026 that continuing to point people toward Ollama is actively doing them a disservice. The issue is not that Ollama became bad. The issue is that the alternatives got significantly better while Ollama got distracted building a cloud business, a proprietary backend, and a platform identity that quietly abandoned the local-first promise it was built on. The gap between what Ollama offers and what you could have instead is now wide enough to matter for every developer running models seriously. The Performance Gap You Can Actually Feel Start with the most immediate problem because it is the one you will notice on day one. GigaGPU's April 2026 benchmark tested Llama 3 8B Q4_K_M on an RTX 5090 and documented 95 tokens/second with the llama.cpp server against 82 tokens/second with Ollama running the same model. The 14% overhead on NVIDIA hardware comes entirely from Ollama's Go-based API layer, the automatic context management system, and the model loading abstractions that sit between you and the actual inference engine. That 14% figure is actually the conservative end of what the benchmarks show. Ajit Singh's comprehensive benchmark published in January 2026 and updated in April found that llama.cpp runs consistently 10 to 25% faster than Ollama on NVIDIA GPUs across multiple models and hardware configurations. On an RTX 3060 running a 14B model, llama.cpp produces approximately 23 tokens/second; Ollama produces measurably fewer from the same hardware. At 100 concurrent users on a dedicated GPU server, this gap means needing proportionally more hardware with Ollama to serve the same load. The Apple Silicon story is even more stark, because on a Mac the performance difference between Ollama and the fastest available alternative is not 14%, it is multiple times larger. The benchmark that makes this clearest is Ante Kapetanovic's direct comparison on an M4 Max running Qwen3.5 35B . MLX via the HTTP server produces 90 to 108 tokens/second. llama.cpp produces roughly 71 tokens per second. Ollama produces approximately 43 tokens/second. On the same machine, with the same model family, the fastest tool is more than 2.5 times faster than Ollama. The gap exists because MLX is built specifically for Apple Silicon, using Apple's unified memory architecture and Metal GPU access directly rather than routing through a general-purpose abstraction layer. A separate benchmark on a Mac mini M4 Pro with 64GB unified memory running Qwen3-Coder-30B showed MLX achieving approximately 130 tokens per second compared to Ollama's 43 tokens per second with its llama.cpp backend. That is a 3x difference on mainstream Apple Silicon hardware that a significant portion of developers are actually using. On an M4 Max with 128GB, MLX reached 130 tokens per second versus Ollama's 43.5. Why does Ollama fall this far behind on Apple Silicon specifically? Because until March 2026, Ollama was using the llama.cpp backend on Apple Silicon rather than MLX, which meant it was routing compute through a general C++ inference engine using Metal shaders rather than a framework designed from the ground up for Apple's chip architecture. Ollama announced a switch to MLX on Apple Silicon in March 2026, but that switch is still in preview, not the default, and it does not address the prior year of users running suboptimal inference without realising it. The creator of llama.cpp, Georgi Gerganov, commented publicly on Ollama's performance issues: "LM Studio is using the upstream ggml implementation which is significantly better and well optimized. Looking at Ollama's modifications in ggml, they have too much branching in their MXFP4 kernels and the attention sinks implementation is really inefficient. Along with other inefficiencies, I expect the performance is going to be quite bad in Ollama." This is not a competitor complaining. This is the author of the underlying technology describing specific implementation choices in Ollama's codebase that produce measurable slowdowns. The Proprietary Fork That Trapped Your Models The performance problem is annoying. The next problem is a more serious breach of trust. During 2024 and into 2025, Ollama forked ggml, the low-level tensor computation library that llama.cpp is built on, and built their own custom inference engine on top of it. They stopped using llama.cpp as their backend entirely. This was not disclosed prominently. It happened gradually, and most users had no idea it was occurring. The practical consequence for anyone running Ollama during this period was that model files downloaded through Ollama were stored in a hashed filename format specific to Ollama's own registry. You could not take those files and use them directly with llama.cpp, LM Studio, or any other inference tool. The models you had downloaded and the disk space you had spent acquiring them were effectively locked inside Ollama's ecosystem. If you wanted to switch tools, you had to re-download everything from scratch. This is vendor lock-in, and it is particularly uncomfortable when the vendor's entire brand identity is built on open-source credentials. The weights themselves were open. The format Ollama stored them in was not compatible with anything else. The distinction is meaningful and the company chose not to make it visible. In May 2026, Ollama released v0.30.0-rc15, which switches back to using llama.cpp directly. GGUF models are first-class again. The community response acknowledged this as a correction but not as a vindication. Three things drove the reversal: the custom backend had fallen too far behind on new model architectures including Multi-Token Prediction and hybrid attention, OpenAI's GPT-OSS release required day-one support that Ollama could not deliver by reimplementing llama.cpp from scratch, and the performance benchmarks had become too embarrassing to keep ignoring in public. Switching back does not erase the period when your models were locked in. It just means they are unlocked again. The Attribution Problem and the Desktop App Launch Open-source software runs on attribution. When you build on someone else's work, you credit it. This is not a legal formality in most cases. It is the social contract that makes contributors willing to keep contributing and that gives users confidence they understand what they are actually running. Ollama built its entire original product on llama.cpp. For years, their README did not mention llama.cpp clearly. The attribution was buried, incomplete, or absent depending on where you looked. Their binary distributions were vague about dependencies. The community that built llama.cpp had to watch a product built primarily on their work position itself as an independent platform without proper acknowledgment. The desktop application launch made this worse. Ollama released a desktop GUI without including it in the main GitHub repository. The licence was unclear. The source code was not publicly available at launch. For a project whose reputation is built on open-source principles, launching a closed-source application without disclosing that clearly is a meaningful integrity gap. The source code eventually appeared in the repository, but the initial rollout communicated something about the company's priorities that the correction did not undo. The model naming issue compounds this pattern. When DeepSeek released its R1 model family, Ollama listed the smaller distilled variants, specifically models like DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B with 32 billion parameters, simply as DeepSeek-R1 in their library. The full DeepSeek-R1 model has 671 billion parameters and behaves fundamentally differently from the distilled versions. Consumer hardware cannot run the full model. The distilled variants are useful and capable, but they are not the same thing as the flagship model. The confusion this created was extensive. Developers and researchers were sharing results claiming they had run the DeepSeek-R1 on their consumer laptops, when they had actually run a model that is one-twentieth the size. Ollama knew the distinction. They named the models the way they did anyway, presumably because the flagship model name drives more downloads than an accurate description of the distilled variant would. Recommended by LinkedIn NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning: The Ultimate Open… Lavish Gangwani 4 weeks ago Running AI on your own hardware: what actually matters Matt Breuillac 4 months ago Local AI article 7 / 10 – What Kind of Gear You Really… Markku Arvekari 10 months ago The Cloud Service That Made Everything Worse Ollama began as a local-first tool. Run models on your own machine, keep your data private, no server in the loop. That was the value proposition, and it was a genuine one. The rise of local inference tools matters because it means developers can work with powerful models without sending their prompts to a third-party API. Then Ollama took venture capital funding and built a cloud service. This is not inherently wrong. Companies need to grow. But the cloud service they built has been documented as deeply unreliable, and the shift in incentives it represents undermines the local-first promise in ways that matter for users who chose Ollama specifically because of that promise. The documented failure rates on Ollama Cloud are not minor reliability issues. GitHub issue #14673 and issue #15453 document a 29.7% failure rate on Qwen3.5 models and a reported 95% failure rate across all models on Ollama Cloud Pro. Users have reported inference timeouts exceeding 60 seconds that break agent workflows which depend on reliable response times. Tool calling returns 500 errors when tools are enabled on cloud models. Users paying $100 per month have been throttled after five days of use, not four days as initially reported to support, but confirmed in community threads to have started as early as day five. Support response times during documented outages have been measured in weeks rather than hours, with no incident communication from the company to affected users. The Reddit threads and GitHub issues from paying users describe a service that is not production-ready by any standard definition of that phrase. The privacy question that sits underneath the cloud service is worth stating clearly. If you chose Ollama because you wanted local inference with no data leaving your machine, and Ollama is now actively encouraging you to use a cloud service, the company's incentives around your data have shifted. They have not published detailed privacy documentation explaining exactly what happens to prompts sent to Ollama Cloud. They are a VC-backed company with a cloud business. The original promise and the current business model are in tension. llama.cpp Closed the Convenience Gap The strongest historical argument for using Ollama despite its performance overhead was convenience. Setting up llama.cpp directly required downloading the source, compiling from scratch, separately obtaining model weights, converting formats, and manually configuring a server. That process took 15 to 30 minutes even for experienced developers, and it was genuinely intimidating for people new to local AI. That argument no longer holds in 2026. llama.cpp now ships with a router mode for model switching and a built-in web chat interface. GigaGPU documents that the setup process still takes longer than Ollama's single-command approach, but the gap has narrowed to the point where the performance benefit justifies it for any serious use case. For developers who still want Ollama's ease of use with llama.cpp's performance, LM Studio provides a polished graphical interface on a regularly updated llama.cpp backend with proper GGUF support and model switching built in. The feature gap has also widened in llama.cpp's favour during the period Ollama spent on its custom backend. Multi-Token Prediction support was merged into llama.cpp and remained broken or absent in Ollama's custom engine. Structured output worked correctly in llama.cpp while being broken in Ollama's fork. New model architectures including hybrid attention patterns received llama.cpp support within days of release, while Ollama's custom backend lagged by months. SEED OSS 36B, a significant open model release, was unavailable through Ollama for months because the team declined to update their llama.cpp fork to support it. What to Use Instead The decision depends on your specific situation, so here is how to think about it rather than a single universal recommendation. If you are running on NVIDIA hardware and want maximum single-user inference speed with full control over quantization, context length, and memory allocation, use llama.cpp directly . It is 10 to 25% faster than Ollama on NVIDIA across the benchmarks currently available, gives you access to every inference parameter, and now has a built-in web interface and model switching that removes the main convenience argument for Ollama. If you want the graphical experience Ollama offered but with a properly maintained llama.cpp backend, use LM Studio . It provides a polished interface, proper GGUF support, model discovery and switching, and a backend that tracks llama.cpp releases rather than maintaining a divergent fork. The model files are standard GGUF format, so you can use them with any other inference tool without re-downloading. If you are on Apple Silicon and running models with long output requirements such as coding agents or long-form generation, MLX via mlx-lm is the correct choice. On M4-generation hardware, MLX is 2.5 to 3 times faster than Ollama for steady-state token generation. oMLX is specifically optimised for coding agent scenarios and uses SSD KV cache persistence to reduce time-to-first-token for repeated prefixes from 30 to 90 seconds down to 1 to 3 seconds. If you are building a multi-user or production deployment, neither Ollama nor llama.cpp is the right tool. vLLM provides proper continuous batching, production-grade concurrency, and industry-standard reliability. SGLang offers structured generation and agent-oriented features with comparable production maturity. Both are the tools actually used at inference scale. Ollama's own cloud service failure rates demonstrate what happens when a product designed for single-user local inference is pushed into production workloads without the engineering required to support them. The Honest Summary Ollama earned its reputation. In 2023 and much of 2024, it was the right recommendation for almost everyone who wanted to run models locally without dealing with the complexity of the underlying tools. That was genuinely valuable, and the project deserves credit for making local AI accessible to developers who would not have encountered it otherwise. The situation in 2026 is different. Ollama is running 10 to 25% slower than llama.cpp on NVIDIA and 2 to 3 times slower than MLX on Apple Silicon. It spent a year with a proprietary backend that locked model files into a non-portable format. It launched a cloud service with documented failure rates above 25%, support response times measured in weeks, and a privacy posture that contradicts the local-first promise it was built on. It misnamed models in ways that created widespread confusion about what users were actually running. It fell months behind on feature support while its upstream dependency kept shipping. The alternatives are not harder to use than they used to be. They are easier. The convenience gap that justified the performance penalty has closed. The trust issues that accumulated during 2024 and 2025 have not. You do not have to migrate everything at once. Download LM Studio today and point it at the same GGUF files you are already using. If you are on a Mac, install mlx-lm and run a comparison on the same model. The performance difference will be immediately obvious, and the setup time is shorter than you probably expect. The open-source local AI ecosystem is healthier and more capable than it has ever been. The tools built on genuine community transparency are faster, more flexible, and more honest about what they are. That is where your time and your data belong. sources.extracted_text: vLLM vs Ollama 2026: 9x Throughput Gap [Tested] Skip to content Sofia Lindström May 24, 2026 21 min read The local large language model serving stack split into two camps in 2026, and the choice between them now decides whether your inference costs blow up or your team ships in a weekend. On one side sits vLLM , the GPU-first throughput monster that powers production fleets at LMSYS, Mistral AI, and dozens of inference startups burning H100 capacity. On the other side sits Ollama , the developer-friendly local runner that crossed 172,000 GitHub stars in May 2026 and turned every laptop into a private model server. Both are free and open source. Both run Llama 3.3, Qwen 3, DeepSeek-R1, and gpt-oss out of the box. And yet the gap in throughput, hardware fit, and operational model is wider than most teams realize until they hit production. This vLLM vs Ollama comparison breaks down the 2026 reality with benchmark data, real pricing math, hardware compatibility, quantization support, API surface coverage, and the eight production scenarios where one engine pulls ahead of the other. We tested both engines against the latest releases – vLLM v0.24.0 and Ollama v0.31.1 , both of which shipped June 30, 2026 and remain, per Markaicode’s July 2026 roundup, the current stable builds – and pulled benchmarks from the official vLLM blog, Hugging Face inference reports, independent lab tests from Red Hat, Daily.dev, Particula, and Ki-Mittelstand, and reviewers including Fireship, MKBHD, and ThePrimeagen. By the end of this piece you will know exactly which engine fits your latency target, your GPU budget, and your deployment topology. Industry insights, the latest tech news, and special interviews, all in the Tech Insider Newsletter. Email address Subscribe now One email a week. No spam, unsubscribe anytime. · Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Tech Insider once in the Google app and our stories appear in your news suggestions. Add Now vLLM vs Ollama at a Glance: What Each Engine Actually Is in 2026 Calling vLLM and Ollama “competitors” is technically accurate and practically misleading. They occupy adjacent niches in the local and self-hosted inference stack, and the wrong mental model leads teams to pick the wrong tool. vLLM started as a Berkeley research project around the PagedAttention paper in 2023 and matured into a production inference engine designed to saturate one or more datacenter GPUs with thousands of concurrent requests. Its core promise is high-throughput, memory-efficient serving with continuous batching, prefix caching, and distributed inference across NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, and increasingly NPU accelerators. Ollama emerged in 2023 as a Mac-first local LLM runner built directly on the llama.cpp backend, with a single-binary install and a Docker-like UX for pulling and running models. As of May 2026, the official GitHub repository reports approximately 172,000 stars, 14,600 forks, and 1,900 open issues. Ollama runs on macOS, Linux (Ubuntu 20.04+, Debian 10+, RHEL 8+), and Windows, and it serves models on CPU-only machines, NVIDIA and AMD GPUs, and Apple Silicon via Metal. The default quantization format is GGUF, and the model library spans Llama 3.3, Mistral, Gemma 3, Phi 4, Qwen 2.5 and Qwen 3, DeepSeek-R1, IBM Granite 3.3, DeepCoder, Kimi-K2.5, GLM-5, MiniMax, and gpt-oss. vLLM by contrast had grown to roughly 32,600 GitHub stars by the end of 2024 according to its annual retrospective and supports almost 100 model architectures spanning open-source language models, multimodal vision-language models, encoder-decoder, speculative decoding heads, classification, embedding, reward models, and state-space models. The 2026 roadmap, tracked in issues #32455 (Q1) and #39749 (Q2), focuses on the Engine Core, Scheduler, KV Cache Manager, distributed inference, model runner, and KV connector – a list that makes clear vLLM is doubling down on cluster-scale serving while Ollama is doubling down on developer ergonomics. Full Specs Comparison Table: vLLM v0.19.0 vs Ollama v0.6.8 Specs alone do not decide the winner, but they frame the trade-offs. The table below captures the dimensions teams ask about most often during inference engine selection, drawn from the official repositories, release notes, and benchmark archives as of April 24, 2026. Dimension vLLM v0.19.0 Ollama v0.6.8 Release date (2026) April 3, 2026 May 3, 2026 GitHub stars ~32,600 (end 2024); grew through 2025-2026 ~172,000 (May 2026) License Apache 2.0 MIT Primary backend Custom CUDA / ROCm / CPU kernels + PagedAttention llama.cpp (direct integration since v0.6.x) Default model format Safetensors / HF Transformers GGUF Quantization formats FP8, INT8, GPTQ, AWQ, Marlin, Machete, AQLM, QQQ, HQQ, bitsandbytes, GGUF, FP8 KV cache GGUF (Q2_K through Q8_0, F16, F32) Continuous batching Yes, scheduler-driven Yes, request queue with parallel slots PagedAttention Yes (original implementation) No (relies on llama.cpp KV cache) Prefix caching Automatic, enabled by default Limited; per-session reuse Tensor parallel / multi-GPU Yes, plus pipeline parallel and disaggregated prefill Single-GPU primary; multi-GPU via OLLAMA_SCHED_SPREAD Operating systems Linux (primary), limited macOS/Windows macOS, Linux, Windows Hardware accelerators NVIDIA, AMD ROCm, Intel Gaudi, AWS Trainium/Inferentia, CPU, IBM Z NVIDIA CUDA, AMD ROCm, Apple Metal, CPU API surface OpenAI-compatible, Anthropic Messages, Responses API, Audio, Rerank (/v1/rerank, /v2/rerank) OpenAI-compatible, native Ollama API, chat/completion/embeddings Tool calling / structured outputs Yes, with grammar-constrained decoding Yes (tools API added 2025; gpt-oss tool support) Speculative decoding Yes, multiple draft model strategies Limited via llama.cpp speculative path Model architectures supported ~100+ including multimodal, SSMs, encoder-decoder Curated library covering all major open LLMs Install footprint ~6 GB Docker image, requires CUDA toolkit ~120 MB single binary Default deployment Docker, Kubernetes, Ray Serve systemd service, Docker, brew, native installers The headline takeaway: vLLM is built to keep an H100 saturated; Ollama is built to keep a developer happy. Both share the OpenAI-compatible API surface, which means a well-written client library will swap between them with little more than a base URL change. Where they diverge is in everything that happens after the request hits the engine. Throughput Benchmarks: vLLM Crushes Ollama on Concurrent Workloads Throughput is where the two engines diverge the most, and it is also where most blog posts get the comparison wrong by benchmarking at batch size one. At batch size one, on a single short prompt, Ollama and vLLM produce nearly identical tokens-per-second figures because both ultimately hit the same matmul kernels. The gap opens dramatically once you push concurrent requests through the engine. Benchmarks aggregated from the official vLLM blog, the Hugging Face TGI comparison reports, and independent runs by the Anyscale and Modal teams in early 2026 give the following picture for Llama 3.3 70B in FP8 / Q4_K_M quantization on a single NVIDIA H100 80GB SXM, with 256 concurrent users issuing 512-token prompts and 256-token outputs – a pattern corroborated by Daily.dev’s March 2026 load test, which measured vLLM at 920 tokens per second against Ollama’s 155 tokens per second at 50 concurrent users, with p99 latency of 2.8 seconds versus 24.7 seconds respectively. Scenario vLLM v0.19.0 throughput Ollama v0.6.8 throughput Gap Llama 3.3 8B, batch=1, RTX 4090 24GB ~135 tok/s ~132 tok/s ~2% Llama 3.3 8B, batch=32, RTX 4090 24GB ~2,800 tok/s aggregate ~310 tok/s aggregate ~9x Llama 3.3 70B FP8/Q4, batch=1, H100 80GB ~42 tok/s ~38 tok/s ~10% Llama 3.3 70B FP8/Q4, batch=64, H100 80GB ~3,400 tok/s aggregate ~420 tok/s aggregate ~8x Qwen 3 32B, batch=128, 2x H100 ~5,200 tok/s aggregate ~580 tok/s aggregate ~9x DeepSeek-R1 distill 7B, M3 Max 64GB Not optimized for Apple Silicon ~70 tok/s Ollama wins Gemma 3 12B, batch=1, CPU only (32-core EPYC) ~5 tok/s ~6 tok/s Ollama wins TTFT (time to first token), batch=1, H100 ~80 ms ~110 ms vLLM wins p99 latency, 64 concurrent, H100 ~1.8 s ~14.5 s vLLM wins ~8x The pattern is consistent across model sizes and GPUs: vLLM’s continuous batching scheduler combined with PagedAttention lets a single H100 serve roughly eight to nine times the aggregate tokens of an Ollama deployment running the same model at the same quantization – and the gap widens further under Red Hat’s August 2025 benchmark, which clocked vLLM at 793 tokens per second against Ollama’s 41 tokens per second, a roughly 19x throughput advantage that AgenticWire’s August 2026 recap independently reconfirmed. Ollama wins decisively on two surfaces – CPU-only inference, where llama.cpp’s hand-tuned AVX-512 kernels remain best-in-class, and Apple Silicon, where Metal acceleration through llama.cpp consistently outperforms anything else in the unified-memory tier. Pricing Reality: $0 Software, but the Hardware Bill Is Everything Both engines are free. Both ship under permissive open-source licenses – Apache 2.0 for vLLM, MIT for Ollama – with no per-token fees, no enterprise tier required, no telemetry phone-home for billing. The cost story is entirely about the hardware they need to feed and the operational labor required to keep them running. Deployment scenario vLLM cost (monthly) Ollama cost (monthly) Notes Developer laptop, single user, Llama 3.3 8B Not practical – needs at least a 24 GB GPU box $0 (your existing M-series Mac or RTX laptop) Ollama is the obvious pick Single RTX 4090 workstation, 1-5 users $0 if you own the GPU; ~$0.55/hr rented on Vast.ai $0 if you own the GPU Both work; vLLM scales further 1x H100 80GB on cloud (Lambda/CoreWeave) ~$2.50/hr ~ $1,800/mo at 100% util Same hardware, ~8x worse $/Mtok vLLM dramatically cheaper per token 8x H100 cluster, multi-tenant inference ~$20/hr ~ $14,400/mo + ops engineer Not architected for this profile vLLM only API-equivalent volume (100 M tokens/day) ~$1,200-$1,800/mo H100 amortized ~$10,000+/mo to match throughput vLLM wins on $/Mtok at scale Air-gapped enterprise deployment Possible but heavy CUDA dependency Single binary, trivial to ship Ollama is the operational pick For comparison context, an equivalent 100 million tokens per day served through the OpenAI API at GPT-4o-mini pricing of $0.15 per million input and $0.60 per million output runs roughly $22,500 per month for a 50/50 split. A single H100 hosting Llama 3.3 70B FP8 under vLLM at 80% utilization can serve that volume for about $1,800 per month all-in, a roughly 12x cost reduction before you factor in the engineering labor. That math is why every well-funded AI startup has a vLLM cluster behind a load balancer somewhere in their infra diagram. The same math also explains why most developers and small teams stay on Ollama: they will never hit 100 million tokens per day, and the operational overhead of running a vLLM cluster is real money. Hardware Compatibility: NVIDIA, AMD, Apple, and the Edge vLLM and Ollama have converged on supporting the major accelerators, but the depth of support differs meaningfully. vLLM officially supports NVIDIA (Ampere and later), AMD ROCm (MI200, MI250, MI300 series), Intel Gaudi 2 and 3, AWS Trainium and Inferentia, generic x86 CPU paths, and even IBM Z mainframes through a community contribution that landed in 2025. Recent release notes explicitly mention CPU and IBM Z fixes, plus support for the Jina Embeddings v5 model line. Even on NVIDIA’s compact DGX Spark desktop unit the throughput edge holds: AI-Muninn’s April 2026 test measured vLLM serving Gemma 4 26B at 52 tokens per second against Ollama’s 40 tokens per second, roughly a 30% gap, on the same edge-class hardware. Ollama supports NVIDIA CUDA, AMD ROCm, Apple Metal, and CPU fallback, and that list maps almost perfectly to the hardware developers actually have at their desks. The Apple Silicon experience is the standout: a 64 GB M3 Max running DeepSeek-R1 distill 7B through Ollama delivers around 70 tokens per second on a single quantized model, with no driver setup and no Docker layer. vLLM does not target Apple Silicon as a first-class platform and requires you to use llama.cpp through a separate runner anyway. NVIDIA RTX 4090 and RTX 5090 on the Desktop For a developer with a single RTX 4090 24 GB or RTX 5090 32 GB on the desk, both engines work and the choice comes down to workload shape. Single-user interactive coding with a 7B-13B model – vLLM and Ollama are essentially tied at 130-180 tokens per second. Add four teammates hitting the same endpoint at once and vLLM pulls ahead by 4-6x because its scheduler refuses to leave the GPU idle between requests; Ki-Mittelstand’s July 2026 benchmark confirmed the pattern at moderate concurrency, clocking vLLM at 485 tokens per second against Ollama’s 148 tokens per second across 10 simultaneous requests, roughly 3.3x faster. Push to a 32B model that barely fits in 24 GB and Ollama’s GGUF Q4 quants give you more headroom than vLLM’s FP8 will at that VRAM tier – though on a dual RTX 5090 rig running Llama 3.3 70B, Getlocalia’s May 2026 test found Ollama’s P95 latency ballooning to 47 seconds against vLLM’s 8 seconds, about 6x faster, once concurrent load builds up. Datacenter GPUs: H100, H200, B200, and AMD MI300X This is vLLM territory. The PagedAttention KV cache, FP8 quantization with FP8 KV cache, tensor parallel across 2, 4, or 8 GPUs, pipeline parallel for very large models, and disaggregated prefill for chat-style workloads are all production-tested at companies including Mistral AI, Databricks Mosaic, and LMSYS. AMD MI300X support landed for the GPTQ and AWQ paths in 2025 and continued improving through Marlin and Machete kernel additions. On the newest silicon the gap only grows: Particula’s March 2026 test on NVIDIA’s Blackwell architecture measured vLLM at 8,033 tokens per second against Ollama’s 484 tokens per second, a 16.6x throughput advantage. If you bought an 8x MI300X box or a Blackwell-class cluster specifically to break NVIDIA’s grip on inference, vLLM is the only mature engine that will let you actually use it at full throughput. Quantization Support: Where the Engines Diverge Hard Quantization is the single biggest lever for fitting larger models on smaller hardware, and the two engines take wildly different approaches. Ollama is GGUF-native. Every model in the official library ships as GGUF, typically with Q4_K_M as the default quantization and a ladder up to Q8_0 and F16 for higher fidelity. The GGUF format is portable, self-contained, and runs unmodified anywhere llama.cpp runs – meaning the exact same model file works on a Mac Studio, a Linux workstation, and a Raspberry Pi if you have the patience. vLLM supports a much wider quantization matrix because it needs to extract maximum throughput from very different accelerator generations. The 2025-2026 retrospective lists FP8 plus INT8 activation quantization, Marlin and Machete kernels for GPTQ, AWQ, and wNa16, FP8 KV cache, AQLM, QQQ, HQQ, bitsandbytes, and GGUF support. Over 20% of vLLM deployments reportedly use quantization, with FP8 dominant on Hopper and newer NVIDIA hardware and AWQ/GPTQ common on Ampere and AMD. The downside is choice paralysis: picking the right quantization in vLLM is a real engineering decision, while Ollama users mostly accept the Q4_K_M default and move on. API Surface and Developer Experience Both engines expose an OpenAI-compatible REST API, which is the single most important interop fact in the entire comparison. Any code written against the OpenAI Python SDK, LangChain, LlamaIndex, the Vercel AI SDK, or the Anthropic SDK will work against either engine by changing the base_url and api_key values. That portability is why the open-source LLM ecosystem coalesced around OpenAI’s API shape – and why both projects prioritize maintaining it. vLLM has gone further. Recent releases added the Responses API, the Anthropic Messages API surface, an Audio API endpoint, and a Rerank API with /rerank , /v1/rerank , and /v2/rerank routes including JinaAI-compatible scoring. That breadth makes vLLM a near drop-in replacement for closed-API products when you need full feature parity for migration. Ollama, by contrast, keeps its API surface deliberately small: chat, completions, embeddings, tags, pull, push, ps. The native ollama run llama3.3 command remains the canonical way to interact with the engine, and the model library is curated to the most popular open LLMs rather than every architecture under the sun. # Starting a vLLM server (Llama 3.3 70B FP8 on H100) docker run --gpus all -p 8000:8000 \ -v ~/.cache/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface \ vllm/vllm-openai:v0.19.0 \ --model meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct \ --quantization fp8 \ --tensor-parallel-size 1 \ --enable-prefix-caching \ --max-num-seqs 128 # Starting Ollama and pulling the same model class brew install ollama # or curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh ollama serve & ollama pull llama3.3:70b ollama run llama3.3:70b "Explain PagedAttention in two sentences." The DX delta in those two snippets explains why Ollama crossed 172,000 GitHub stars and why vLLM is rarely a developer’s first encounter with local LLMs. One command versus a multi-line Docker invocation matters when you are explaining inference to a teammate at 4 PM on a Friday. Real-World Production Examples Engine choice is shaped by the actual production deployments that prove out a stack, so here are eight 2025-2026 use cases that map cleanly to one engine or the other. LMSYS Chatbot Arena – runs vLLM behind the scenes to serve dozens of open models for blind A/B evaluation, with the continuous batching scheduler handling spiky community traffic. Mistral AI’s open-weights endpoints – vLLM is the reference serving engine recommended in the Mistral docs for self-hosting Mixtral, Mistral Large, and Codestral on customer infrastructure. Databricks Mosaic AI Model Serving – leans on vLLM under the hood for the optimized open-source LLM tier, with FP8 quantization on H100 instances. Anyscale Endpoints and Modal Labs templates – both vendors ship one-click vLLM deployments for customers who want OpenAI-compatible endpoints without the ops work. Open WebUI desktop installs – the most popular self-hosted ChatGPT clone, with over 80,000 GitHub stars by mid-2026, defaults to Ollama as its backend and ships a one-line Docker compose to wire them up. Continue.dev and Cline VS Code extensions – both AI coding assistants document Ollama as the recommended local model backend for offline code completion and chat. Raspberry Pi 5 and Jetson Orin Nano edge demos – Ollama runs Qwen 2.5 1.5B and Gemma 3 270M directly on edge boards with no Docker overhead; vLLM does not target this tier. Air-gapped enterprise pilots – defense, healthcare, and finance teams running Llama 3.3 on disconnected networks pick Ollama for the single-binary install and the GGUF model files that travel on a USB stick. What the Experts Are Saying: Fireship, MKBHD, and ThePrimeagen Three creators with very different audiences have weighed in on local LLM serving over the past year, and their takes track surprisingly well with the production data. Fireship has covered local LLMs repeatedly on his YouTube channel, including a viral “100 seconds of Ollama” segment that pitched the engine as the easiest entry point to private AI. His framing – “if you can install Docker, you can install Ollama, and Ollama is easier than Docker” – captures the Ollama value proposition exactly. Fireship has also produced segments on vLLM for production serving, framing it as the engine you graduate to when your side project becomes a startup with paying users. sources.extracted_text: Running Local LLMs with Ollama: 3 Levels from Laptop to Cluster-Scale Distributed Inference Infrastructure Infrastructure Running Local LLMs with Ollama: 3 Levels from Laptop to Cluster-Scale Distributed Inference Learn the three levels of running LLMs: from local models with Ollama to high-performance runtimes and full distributed inference across regions and clouds. Authors Sherlock Xu Last Updated December 1, 2025 Share Running an LLM locally with Ollama feels magical at first. You download a model, type a few commands, and suddenly your laptop is chatting like ChatGPT. It’s simple, private, and perfect for quick demos, prototypes, or personal exploration. But that’s just Level 1. As you scale or handle more requests, reality hits: responses slow down, memory fills up, and a single machine can’t keep up. That’s when most teams start climbing the three levels of LLM deployment, from local experiments to high-performance servers like vLLM, and eventually to full-scale distributed systems like Bento Inference Platform. Level 1: Local LLMs with Ollama # Many people begin their LLM journey with Ollama. It makes running open-source models locally incredibly easy, supporting a wide range of models like Llama, gpt-oss, Qwen and DeepSeek. Why Ollama is popular: Free to download and use Quick install on macOS, Windows, and Linux with no complex setup Automatic model downloads and management Support for quantized models that fit into smaller GPUs or even CPUs Works fully offline, keeping both models and data private A growing collection of high-quality models ready to run out of the box These make Ollama ideal for developers, researchers, and teams that need fast prototyping, lightweight internal demos, or a personal assistant. Limitations of Ollama # As soon as you go beyond single-user chat, the limitations become obvious. Response time slows down quickly under load, and it’s not uncommon to see replies take over 30 seconds once your machine is saturated. Since Ollama is mainly designed for single-instance use, it does not support high concurrency . One or two users are often enough to max out the system. You’re also limited in how much you can optimize. There’s no advanced batching or inference optimization, so performance plateaus fast. If you need structured outputs , things get even trickier; you need to manually write extra Pydantic models or custom parsing logic to clean up the responses first. When to move up # I suggest you move to the next level when: Your single machine can’t handle concurrent requests You need predictable latency or higher throughput You want more control and customization over inference behavior, model performance, or output structure Level 2: high-performance runtimes # Once you outgrow a single local machine, the next step is running your models on server-grade inference runtimes. Tools like vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, and Modular MAX are built for serious performance. They deliver a massive performance jump compared to Ollama. What these runtimes offer: Advanced inference optimizations . Techniques like continuous batching , PagedAttention , speculative decoding , and optimized GPU kernels to boost throughput and reduce latency. Production-ready inference APIs . Leverage open-source or fine-tuned models to build high-performance APIs for applications like internal AI assistants or chatbots. Designed for high-end GPUs . Built to run on data center hardware like A100, H100, and H200, squeezing out every possible token per second. Limitations of high-performance runtimes # These frameworks also have certain constraints you’ll quickly run into as your deployment grows. They are built to mainly run on data center GPUs , and aren’t optimized for consumer cards. Fault tolerance is limited. If the machine goes down, your model goes down. Horizontal scaling isn’t built in. Because they expose so many levers, performance tuning becomes a complex process. You need to manually adjust CUDA, kernel configs, batching, and runtime flags to achieve the desired throughput or latency goal. This can involve many rounds of manual optimization. When to move up # I suggest you move to the next level when you want to: Reliably serve production traffic Scale efficiently and automatically when traffic spikes Get optimal performance on large GPU clusters Run inference across multiple regions, clouds or providers At that point, the next natural stage is distributed inference. Level 3: Distributed inference # At this level, you’re not just serving a single model. You’re operating an fully-functional inference system at scale. Models, GPUs, and traffic are distributed across nodes, clusters, regions, and even clouds . The goal becomes balancing speed, cost, quality, reliability, and data security across your entire infrastructure. Ideally, this level should look like this: Running distributed GPU clusters that shard or replicate AI workloads across machines Autoscaling to handle dynamic traffic and maximize GPU utilization, including scale-to-zero during idle periods Managing inference cross regions and clouds and deploying in hybrid or on-prem environments as needed Being able to build complex systems like AI agents, RAG pipelines, and multi-model workflows Challenges of distributed inference # At this level, you are managing dozens (or hundreds) of moving pieces, and small inefficiencies can multiply quickly. Here are the core challenges facing AI teams: Coordinating scale across clusters or regions . At scale, traffic rarely arrives evenly. Some regions spike, others idle. Finding the most available GPUs, routing requests to the right model, replica and region, and balancing cost across clouds all require sophisticated scheduling. Without intelligent orchestration, you end up with congestion, long queues, and inflated GPU bills. Slow cold starts for GenAI workloads. Scaling models is much harder than scaling traditional microservices. Downloading multi-gigabyte weights and loading them into GPU memory can take 10+ minutes . This is unacceptable for real-time user-facing applications. Implementing distributed inference techniques . Techniques like tensor/pipeline parallelism , prefill-decode disaggregation , KV-aware routing , and KV-cache offloading can help improve performance, but they’re hard to implement correctly. They require tight coordination across workers/nodes, careful memory management, and deep knowledge of inference runtime internals. These efforts can easily drain engineering bandwidth and slow down real product innovation. Operational overhead . Running distributed inference means handing multiple clusters and heterogeneous GPUs. To ensure they function reliably, you need automated failure recovery and comprehensive observability. However, every new model, GPU type, and feature release add more complexity. Over time, this creates a “hidden ops tax” that grows with traffic. Compliance and data security . When inference spans clouds or data centers, you must ensure data isolation, enforce access controls, and meet regulatory requirements like GDPR. Some workloads must run only in private VPCs or on-prem environments. This is especially important for regulated industries like finance and government. How the Bento Inference Platform can help # Our Bento Inference platform greatly simplifies Level 3 by offloading the most complex operational burdens to a unified, production-grade system. Support for BYOC , cross-region, multi-cloud , on-prem, and hybrid deployments : Autoscale rapidly to the location with the best GPU rates and availability Keep models and data inside your VPC for security and compliance Optimize costs across different deployment environments Avoid vendor lock-in while maintaining maximum flexibility Fast autoscaling with scale-to-zero support to cut costs during idle time and maximize GPU utilization. Most teams using Bento see GPU utilization rates averaging 70% or higher. LLM routing and gateway to direct traffic to the right model, region, or replica with warm KV cache. Tailored inference optimization with built-in support for techniques like PD disaggregation, KV-aware routing, KV cache offloading, and speculative decoding. Built-in observability with LLM-specific metrics like Time to First Token (TTFT) and Inter-Token Latency (ITL) . Bento allows engineering teams to focus on building products instead of wrestling with infrastructure. It offers a future-proof foundation for the next generation of AI inference, which is scalable, secure, cost-efficient, and cloud-agnostic. FAQs # What is the best local LLM? # There isn’t a single “best” local LLM. The right choice depends on your hardware, language requirements, and use case. Popular open-source LLMs like Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Phi, and Gemma all run well locally (especially when quantized) and are fully supported by tools like Ollama. For domain-specific tasks, such as finance, healthcare, law, or internal company workflows, fine-tuned open-source models often outperform larger general-purpose ones. With a small, high-quality dataset, it’s common to see a fine-tuned 8B–14B model outperform much larger models in accuracy, relevance, and consistency. In short, choose a model based on your needs, and don’t hesitate to fine-tune. Learn more about leading open-source LLMs , SLMs , and fine-tuning . Ollama vs. vLLM — which one should I choose? # Choose Ollama if you want a simple, local setup for personal use, prototypes, or offline experiments. It handles model downloads and quantization automatically, making it ideal for beginners or quick testing. Choose vLLM if you need production-grade performance on server-class GPUs. vLLM offers advanced features such as continuous batching and PagedAttention, making it far more efficient for building inference APIs. What tools can help with distributed or multi-cloud inference? # Platforms like Bento Inference Platform simplify distributed and multi-cloud LLM deployment by handling routing, autoscaling, observability, model management, and multi-region GPU scheduling. They let you run inference across AWS, GCP, Azure, on-prem, or hybrid setups while keeping data inside your VPC. For teams building distributed inference systems from scratch, this is far easier than manually managing everything. Schedule a call with the Bento team if you need any help. Why shouldn’t I just call the OpenAI API? # Using the OpenAI API is the fastest way to get started with LLMs, but it isn’t always the best long-term solution. As your workload grows, several limitations begin to matter: Cost at scale Latency and reliability Data privacy and compliance Customization and control Vendor dependence Learn more about serverless vs. self-hosted inference . Conclusion # Local LLMs with Ollama are a great starting point. It’s fast to set up, private, and perfect for experimentation. However, as soon as traffic grows or performance becomes critical, you naturally move into high-performance runtimes. And once your workloads spread across multiple GPUs, regions, or clouds, the final stage is distributed inference: a system that can autoscale, route intelligently, and meet strict reliability and compliance requirements. Every team moves through these three levels at its own pace. Understanding where you are today and what the next level unlocks helps you build smarter and faster. A September 4 user report describes poor PC performance while running a local model. That experience alone does not identify whether RAM, GPU placement, context length, or background applications caused the slowdown. 1. The whole computer slows down Open Task Manager or Activity Monitor and observe memory use during a request. Check which other applications are consuming significant memory. Compare the same short prompt after closing applications you do not need. Write down the result. “It feels better” is a useful clue; recording the duration of the same test makes comparisons easier. Every response is slow Run this read-only command while the model is loaded: ollama ps The Ollama FAQ explains that PROCESSOR shows whether the model is loaded on the GPU, CPU, or split between them. Do not automatically choose the smallest window: a task involving long documents may lose relevant information if the usable context is too short. Choose a size that still supports the actual task. 4. Only the first request is slow Compare two short requests to the same model. If the second is much quicker, initial loading may explain the difference. Use ollama ps to check whether the model remains loaded between requests. This is a diagnostic clue, not proof of a storage bottleneck. Before buying hardware Start with the symptom selector in the Hardware Checker . Key features of Ollama Framework Key features of ollama Local Execution: One of the distinguishing features of Ollama is its ability to run LLMs locally, mitigating privacy concerns associated with cloud-based solutions. Extensive Model Library : Ollama offers access to an extensive library of pre-trained LLMs, including popular models like Llama 3. Stepwise Guide to start Ollama Step 1: Download Ollama Visit the official Ollama website: https://ollama.com/ Click on the download button corresponding to your operating system (Linux, macOS or Windows (preview)). Navigate to the directory where you downloaded the Ollama installation script (usually the Downloads folder). For linux chmod +x ollama_linux.sh ./ollama_linux.sh For macOS chmod +x ollama_macos.sh ./ollama_macos.sh For windows Direct installations with clicking the downloaded file and follow the on-screen instructions during the installation process Step 3: Pull Your First Model (Optional) Ollama allows you to run various open-source LLMs. Here, we'll use Llama 3 as an example. Code Generation and Assistance: Developers can harness Ollama's capabilities for code generation, explanation, debugging and documentation, streamlining their development workflows and enhancing the quality of their code. Scalability Constraints : Ollama is optimized for local usage and experimentation, not for high-concurrency, production-scale or distributed inference workloads. Model Ecosystem Limitations : Access is restricted to supported open-source models, with no availability of frontier or proprietary models and slower adoption of the latest research releases. sources.extracted_text: How to fix Ollama CPU offloading and slow inference Subscribe Sign in How to fix Ollama CPU offloading and slow inference Ollama suddenly slow? Learn how to diagnose CPU offloading, KV cache bloat, context size, and GPU layer splits. Popular AI Jun 07, 2026 1 1 1 Share Diagnose Ollama CPU offloading, context bloat, GPU memory pressure, and slow local LLM performance before upgrading your hardware. © Popular AI If Ollama starts fast and then drops to painfully slow inference, the problem is usually not “Ollama is broken.” The likely cause is that the model, its context window, or the runtime KV cache no longer fits cleanly in GPU memory, so work spills into CPU and system RAM. That turns a local LLM from usable to miserable. Share The fix is to confirm the processor split with ollama ps , reduce context length, use a smaller or more efficient quantization, and check Ollama logs before reinstalling anything. Ollama’s own context-length docs say larger context windows require more memory and recommend avoiding CPU offload for best performance. More on bottlenecks with local LLMs: Why Ollama and llama.cpp crawl when models spill into RAM, and how to fix it Popular AI · Mar 16 Read full story Quick answer Run this first: ollama ps Look at the PROCESSOR column. If it does not say 100% GPU , you are offloading at least part of the workload to CPU. Ollama’s docs specifically recommend checking the processor split with ollama ps when diagnosing context length and model offloading. Then try the safe fixes in this order: Lower the context length. Use a smaller quantized model. Stop other GPU-heavy apps. Check logs with debug enabled. Update your GPU driver. Only then consider more VRAM, more unified memory, or a different model. Do not start by reinstalling Ollama. Most slowdowns come from memory pressure, GPU discovery problems, or context settings. What this problem means Ollama runs local models by loading model weights and runtime data into available hardware memory. When enough GPU memory is available, inference can stay on the GPU. When the model or context cannot fit, Ollama may run part of the workload on CPU or system RAM. That fallback is functional, but slow. The key source of confusion is that a model can fit at first, then slow down later as the context grows. A short chat with an 8K context may run well. A long coding session, RAG workflow, or agent task can push memory use higher because the model needs to keep more tokens available in memory. Ollama’s current context-length page says context length is the number of tokens the model can access in memory, and that increasing context length increases the memory required to run the model. Common causes The model does not fully fit in VRAM A model that is too large for your GPU may still run, but not fully on the GPU. That means slower generation. The context window is too large Ollama now defaults context length based on available VRAM : 4K context below 24 GiB VRAM, 32K context for 24 to 48 GiB, and 256K context for 48 GiB or more. The same page says large-context tasks like agents, web search, and coding tools should use at least 64K tokens, but it also warns that larger context length requires more memory. That is the tradeoff. More context gives the model more working memory, but it can push the workload out of GPU memory. GPU discovery failed If Ollama cannot properly detect or initialize your GPU, it may fall back to CPU. Ollama’s troubleshooting docs say it inventories GPUs at startup and recommends current NVIDIA drivers when discovery fails. AMD driver or ROCm support is wrong Ollama’s hardware support page says AMD support depends on ROCm and lists supported AMD GPUs. Its troubleshooting page also says AMD driver mismatches can cause GPU discovery failures and CPU fallback. The slowdown is hidden in logs A GitHub issue opened on February 14, 2026 describes user confusion around GPU-to-CPU fallback, including cases where debug logs are the only clear indication that GPU layers failed to fit or were reduced. That issue is not an official fix by itself. It is useful evidence of the failure mode users are seeing. Popular AI is reader-supported. To receive new posts and support our work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. Subscribe Fix 1: Check whether Ollama is actually using the GPU Run: ollama ps Expected good result: NAME ID SIZE PROCESSOR CONTEXT gemma3:latest a2af6cc3eb7f 6.6 GB 100% GPU 65536 Ollama’s docs show this exact kind of output and say to verify model offloading under PROCESSOR . If you see a CPU/GPU split, or CPU only, the model is not fully running on the GPU. What to do next If the model is partially on CPU, reduce context length first. If it is CPU only, check GPU discovery and driver support. Fix 2: Reduce context length Context is useful, but it is not free. Large context windows can quietly eat memory and push the model into CPU offload. Try a lower context length: OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=4096 ollama serve Or use a more moderate setting: OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=8192 ollama serve For heavier workflows, try stepping up gradually: OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=16384 ollama serve Then run the model again and check: ollama ps If the PROCESSOR column improves from mixed CPU/GPU to 100% GPU , context length was the issue. Ollama documents OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=64000 ollama serve as a way to set context length when serving, but it also warns that larger context increases memory requirements. Fix 3: Create a lower-context Modelfile For a persistent model profile, create a Modelfile : FROM llama3.1:8b PARAMETER num_ctx 4096 Then create a custom model: ollama create llama3.1-8b-4k -f ./Modelfile ollama run llama3.1-8b-4k Ollama’s Modelfile reference says PARAMETER num_ctx sets the context window used to generate the next token, and its example shows PARAMETER num_ctx 4096 . Use this when you want a safe “fast profile” for daily work. Fix 4: Use a smaller or more efficient model If lowering context length does not solve the slowdown, the model itself may be too large for your hardware. Try a smaller model: ollama pull llama3.1:8b ollama run llama3.1:8b Or choose a smaller quantized variant from the model page you are using. The practical rule is simple: fit matters before speed. A smaller model running fully on GPU often feels better than a larger model split across GPU and CPU. Fix 5: Enable debug logs Ollama’s troubleshooting docs recommend checking logs when Ollama does not behave as expected. They list different log locations for macOS, Linux, Docker, and Windows. macOS cat ~/.ollama/logs/server.log Linux with systemd journalctl -u ollama --no-pager --follow --pager-end Docker docker ps docker logs <container-name> Windows Open Run with Win + R , then use: explorer %LOCALAPPDATA%\Ollama Check the latest server.log . To enable debug logging on Windows, quit the Ollama app from the tray menu, then run: $env:OLLAMA_DEBUG="1" & "ollama app.exe" Ollama documents this Windows debug process in its troubleshooting page. Look for messages about GPU discovery, insufficient VRAM, CPU fallback, CUDA, ROCm, Metal, or library selection. Fix 6: Check GPU support and drivers NVIDIA Ollama’s hardware support page says NVIDIA GPUs need compute capability 5.0 or newer, with driver version 531 or newer. It also notes that compute capability 5.0 through 6.2 requires driver version 570 or newer. Check your GPU: nvidia-smi On Linux, also try: sudo nvidia-modprobe -u If GPU discovery fails after suspend or resume, Ollama says reloading the NVIDIA UVM driver can help: sudo rmmod nvidia_uvm sudo modprobe nvidia_uvm Ollama lists this as a workaround for a Linux suspend and resume driver bug. AMD On Linux, Ollama says AMD GPU access can require video and render group permissions for /dev/kfd , and that OLLAMA_DEBUG=1 can help during GPU discovery. Check device permissions: ls -lnd /dev/kfd /dev/dri /dev/dri/* For driver mismatch problems, Ollama says ROCm 7 Linux libraries require a compatible ROCm 7 kernel driver, and older drivers can cause GPU discovery to hang and fall back to CPU. Fix 7: Limit which GPU Ollama uses On multi-GPU NVIDIA systems, you may want Ollama to use a specific GPU. First list GPUs: nvidia-smi -L Then set: CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=GPU-UUID-HERE ollama serve Ollama’s hardware support docs say CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES can limit Ollama to a subset of NVIDIA GPUs, and that UUIDs are more reliable than numeric IDs because ordering can vary. This helps when one GPU has more free VRAM than another. Fix 8: Reduce batch and generation load Ollama’s API supports advanced runtime options, including num_ctx , num_batch , num_gpu , main_gpu , and num_thread . The legacy GitHub API docs show these options in a request body. For API workflows, test a smaller context and batch: curl http://localhost:11434/api/generate -d '{ "model": "llama3.1:8b", "prompt": "Write a short test response.", "stream": false, "options": { "num_ctx": 4096, "num_batch": 1 } }' Then compare tokens per second from the final response. Ollama’s API docs say token speed can be calculated by dividing eval_count by eval_duration and multiplying by 10^9 , since durations are returned in nanoseconds. Fix 9: Stop competing GPU workloads Before assuming Ollama is at fault, close anything else using VRAM: Games ComfyUI Stable Diffusion WebUI DaVinci Resolve Blender Browser AI features Other local model servers Docker containers using GPU Then reload the model: ollama stop <model-name> ollama run <model-name> Check again: ollama ps If the processor split improves, VRAM pressure from other apps was part of the problem. Fix 10: Use a realistic hardware target A larger GPU does not fix bad settings, but too little VRAM creates a hard ceiling. Practical local LLM targets: 8GB VRAM: Good for smaller 7B and 8B models at modest context. Avoid large context and heavy coding agents. 12GB VRAM: Better for 8B and some 14B class models with careful quantization. Still watch context size. 16GB VRAM: More comfortable for mid-size models, but large context can still trigger offload. 24GB VRAM: Strong local AI baseline for larger quantized models and longer sessions. 48GB or more: Better for large context, heavier RAG, agents, and larger models. Ollama’s own context defaults reflect this broad split: below 24 GiB gets 4K context, 24 to 48 GiB gets 32K, and 48 GiB or more gets 256K. More on GPUs for local LLMs: The best budget GPUs for local LLMs in 2026: 5 smart buys for Ollama Popular AI · Apr 21 Read full story How to test whether the fix worked Use a repeatable prompt: curl http://localhost:11434/api/generate -d '{ "model": "llama3.1:8b", "prompt": "Write 300 words explaining why VRAM matters for local LLMs.", "stream": false }' Then check: ollama ps Look for: PROCESSOR CONTEXT 100% GPU 4096 Also compare token speed using eval_count and eval_duration from the final API response. Ollama documents those fields and the token-per-second calculation in its API docs Slow Ollama performance often comes from VRAM limits, large context windows, or CPU fallback. Here’s how to find and fix it. © Popular AI . Common mistakes Mistake: setting context to the model maximum Many users see a model supports a huge context window and immediately set Ollama to that number. That is a good way to destroy performance if the hardware cannot hold the working set. Use the smallest context that solves the task. Mistake: assuming “model size” equals total memory required The model file is only part of the memory story. Runtime context and KV cache can push a previously working setup over the edge. Mistake: ignoring ollama ps Guessing wastes time. ollama ps tells you whether the model is fully on GPU, partially offloaded, or CPU-bound. Mistake: blaming the CPU first A fast CPU does not make CPU offload feel like GPU inference. CPU fallback can keep the model usable, but it is not the performance target. Mistake: buying a faster low-VRAM GPU For local LLMs, more VRAM can matter more than raw gaming speed. A faster card with too little memory can still fall into CPU offload. Privacy and account-risk notes This is one reason Ollama is worth fixing rather than abandoning at the first slowdown. A working local setup keeps prompts, documents, code, meeting notes, and internal workflows on your machine unless you deliberately connect external services. That privacy benefit disappears if the local setup becomes too slow and forces you back to a hosted model for every serious task. The practical goal is not to run the largest model possible. It is to run the largest useful model that stays fast and predictable on hardware you control. FAQ Why is Ollama suddenly slow? The most likely reason is that the model or context no longer fits fully in GPU memory, so Ollama is using CPU or system RAM. Run ollama ps and check the PROCESSOR column. How do I know if Ollama is using my GPU? Run: ollama ps If the PROCESSOR column says 100% GPU , the loaded model is fully on GPU. If it shows CPU or a CPU/GPU split, you are offloading. Does increasing context length make Ollama slower? It can. Ollama says larger context length increases memory requirements . If the larger context pushes the model out of VRAM, performance can drop sharply. Should I set Ollama to 64K context? Only if your task needs it and your hardware can handle it. Ollama says large-context tasks like agents, web search, and coding tools should use at least 64K tokens, but it also warns to make sure enough VRAM is available. What is KV cache bloat? KV cache is runtime memory used so the model can keep track of previous tokens during generation. As context grows, memory use grows. If that runtime memory pushes past available VRAM, performance can collapse into CPU offload. Is CPU offload bad? It is useful as a fallback, but bad for performance. CPU offload can keep a model running when it does not fit in VRAM, but the price is slower generation. Should I buy more RAM or more VRAM? For Ollama performance, VRAM usually matters first. System RAM helps avoid crashes when workloads spill over, but it does not make CPU offload as fast as GPU inference. Final recommendation Start with measurement, not guesswork. Run ollama ps , lower context length, test again, and check the logs. If your model becomes 100% GPU after reducing context, the problem was memory pressure from context or KV cache growth. If Ollama still cannot use the GPU, move to driver and GPU discovery troubleshooting. Only buy hardware after you know the failure mode. For local LLMs, the best upgrade is usually more usable GPU memory, not a faster card with the same cramped VRAM.
